framework: Nielsen's 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design
author: Jakob Nielsen
note: The `definition` field paraphrases Nielsen's published heuristic. The `static_page_test` field is study-authored operational guidance for a static 2-page slice.

heuristics.title: Visibility of system status
heuristics.definition: The design should always keep users informed about what is going on, through appropriate feedback within a reasonable amount of time.
heuristics.static_page_test: Loading, submission, selection and navigation states are visibly communicated; the user is never left guessing whether an action registered.

heuristics.title: Match between the system and the real world
heuristics.definition: The design should speak the users' language, using words, phrases and concepts familiar to the user rather than internal jargon, and follow real-world conventions so information appears in a natural and logical order.
heuristics.static_page_test: Labels, categories and ordering use the vocabulary of the site's domain and audience, not developer or internal terminology.

heuristics.title: User control and freedom
heuristics.definition: Users often perform actions by mistake. They need a clearly marked emergency exit to leave the unwanted action without having to go through an extended process.
heuristics.static_page_test: Cancel, back, close and undo are available and obvious wherever an action can be started.

heuristics.title: Consistency and standards
heuristics.definition: Users should not have to wonder whether different words, situations or actions mean the same thing. Follow platform and industry conventions.
heuristics.static_page_test: Navigation, control styling, terminology and layout behave the same way on every page of the slice.

heuristics.title: Error prevention
heuristics.definition: Good error messages are important, but the best designs carefully prevent problems from occurring in the first place.
heuristics.static_page_test: Constraints, sensible defaults, format hints and confirmation prevent errors before they happen.

heuristics.title: Recognition rather than recall
heuristics.definition: Minimise the user's memory load by making elements, actions and options visible. The user should not have to remember information from one part of the interface to another.
heuristics.static_page_test: Needed information is visible at the point of use rather than something the user must carry in their head.

heuristics.title: Flexibility and efficiency of use
heuristics.definition: Shortcuts may speed up the interaction for the expert user, so that the design can cater to both inexperienced and experienced users.
heuristics.static_page_test: Accelerators, shortcuts or alternate paths exist for frequent tasks without obstructing first-time users.

heuristics.title: Aesthetic and minimalist design
heuristics.definition: Interfaces should not contain information which is irrelevant or rarely needed. Every extra unit of information competes with the relevant units and diminishes their relative visibility.
heuristics.static_page_test: Content earns its place; added help text, labels or affordances do not bury the primary task.

heuristics.title: Help users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors
heuristics.definition: Error messages should be expressed in plain language (no error codes), precisely indicate the problem, and constructively suggest a solution.
heuristics.static_page_test: Errors say what went wrong, where, and what to do about it, in plain language.

heuristics.title: Help and documentation
heuristics.definition: It is best if the system does not need any additional explanation. However, it may be necessary to provide documentation to help users understand how to complete their tasks.
heuristics.static_page_test: Help is findable at the point of need, task-oriented and concrete.
